sources.citation: Usher, Timothy. n.d. [last modified 2024-06-25]. Bogaia. Newguineaworld (UZH DokuWiki),https://newguineaworld.linguistik.uzh.ch/families/trans-new-guinea/duna-bogaia/bogaia
sources.note: Phonology section reads in full: 'There is no published phonology of Bogaya.' Sources listed: Franklin (ed. 1973: 589) 98 terms; Voorhoeve (1975: 396) pronouns; Shaw (1986: 69) 99 terms; Seeland (2007) Bogaia affixes and Seeland (2007) grammar of Bogaia, both '(unobtained)'. Nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Pawley, Andrew & Harald Hammarström. 2018. The Trans New Guinea family. In Bill Palmer (ed.), The languages and linguistics of the New Guinea area, 21-195. De Gruyter Mouton. Sec. 2.3.1.9 Duna-Bogaya.
sources.note: Documentation line: 'Bogaya [boq] 300; wordlist: Franklin 1973a, Shaw 1986'. Nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Hammarström, Harald & Sebastian Nordhoff. 2012. The languages of Melanesia: quantifying the level of coverage. Online appendix (Bogaya entry).
sources.note: Bogaya [boq]: Clancy 1962, Sillitoe 1993, Sillitoe 1995 -- all tagged ethnographic. No linguistic description.

sources.citation: San Roque, Lila & Robyn Loughnane. 2012. Inheritance, contact and change in the New Guinea Highlands evidentiality area. Language & Linguistics in Melanesia, Special Issue 2012 Part II (Harald Hammarstrom & Wilco van den Heuvel eds., History, contact and classification of Papuan languages), 397-427. ISSN 0023-1959. (MPG.PuRe item_1690284, public file; ANU Open Research hdl 1885/733803690, bitstream restricted)
sources.note: Nothing on Bogaia prosody. The only prosodic sentence is generic and names no language: 'Tone is contrastive in some languages, but in the present study we focus on segmental content only.' (p. 400). Bogaia content = evidential enclitics =ki (visual) / =ai (sensory) in Table 3, ex. (18) kolo ta yugu-si-ki 'Kolo is planting taro. (I see him)' (BOGAIA Seeland 2007a), the 'pig is running away' =ai example (Seeland 2007a), Table 6 perception verbs Bogaia haga 'see', wagi 'hear', ?ti 'say', the remark that Bogaia and Duna 'do not appear to share any evidential markers', an endnote on the reported…

sources.citation: San Roque, Lila & Robyn Loughnane. 2012. The New Guinea Highlands evidentiality area. Linguistic Typology 16(1): 111-167.
sources.note: Uses Seeland's Bogaia material (evidential suffixes); the Bogaia examples may show how Seeland transcribes accent, and its bibliography gives the fullest citation of the Seeland mss.

sources.citation: Strathern, Andrew J. & Pamela J. Stewart. 2010. The appearing and disappearing world of the Bogaiya: a corner of Papua New Guinea cultural history. In Kenneth A. McElhanon & Ger Reesink (eds.), A mosaic of languages and cultures: studies celebrating the career of Karl J. Franklin (SIL e-Books 19), 399-407. Dallas: SIL International.
sources.note: Nothing. Read in full from the mirror copy (text, 9 pp.); zero hits for stress/tone/tonal/pitch/accent/syllable/phonology/vowel/consonant/orthography/intonation/prosody; footnote 2 mentions the authors collected language materials in fieldwork but none are presented.

sources.citation: The Rosetta Project. 2010. Bogaya Swadesh List. Internet Archive item rosettaproject_boq_swadesh-1.
sources.note: Two Bogaya forms per gloss, matching the Franklin 1973 and Shaw 1986 lists; a handful of forms carry grave accents (nò, tòua, òghòpi, hèi) of unstated meaning. No source given, no statement.

sources.citation: San Roque, Lila. 2008. An introduction to Duna grammar. PhD thesis, Australian National University. Sec. 1.1.2 p. 7, sec. 2.1 pp. 32-33, references p. 498.
sources.note: p. 7: 'Dan Seeland, one of the founders of the mission station at Ekali/Agali.., has produced a description of Bogaia phonology and grammar (Seeland 2007ab).' Footnote: the author did 'a very small amount of language research with Bogaia speakers (not presented in this thesis)'. pp. 32-33: Duna word-initial /r/ corresponds to Bogaia [t]; Duna aspirated vs unaspirated velars correspond to Bogaia /h/ vs /k/. Nothing on Bogaia stress. References p. 498: Seeland, D. (2007a) Bogaia Affixes; (2007b) Bogaia Grammar -- unpublished manuscripts.

sources.citation: Carrington, Lois. 1996. A linguistic bibliography of the New Guinea area. Pacific Linguistics D-90 (index entries for Bogaya/Bogaia)
sources.note: Index: 'Bogaya (W Prov; also Bogaia) Shaw 1973, 1973, Sillitoe n.d., W&H 1981' and 'Bogaia (also Bogaya) Sillitoe 1994'. Sillitoe 1994 Oceania Monograph 44 flagged as containing a list of plant names (p. 11ff). No linguistic description listed.

sources.citation: Shaw, R. Daniel. 1986. The Bosavi language family. Papers in New Guinea Linguistics 24, 45-76. Pacific Linguistics A-70. Appendix B (languages surrounding the Bosavi family), Bogaya list, p. 69.
sources.note: 100-item phonetic wordlist (vowel-quality symbols, length, some nasalisation); no stress marks and no statement about stress.

sources.citation: Voorhoeve, C. L. 1975. Central and western Trans-New Guinea Phylum languages. In S. A. Wurm (ed.), New Guinea area languages and language study, vol. 1, 345-459. Pacific Linguistics C-38. Sec. 2.6.2.2.6.7.2 Bogaya, p. 396.
sources.note: 'Two wordlists were the only data available to the writer'; gives pronouns, three verb forms, one SOV sentence. No phoneme inventory, nothing on stress. (The neighbouring Duna sketch p. 395 says Duna 'is probably tonal' -- about Duna, not Bogaya.)

sources.citation: Franklin, Karl J. & C. L. Voorhoeve. 1973. Chapter 4: Languages near the intersection of the Gulf, Southern Highlands and Western Districts. In Karl J. Franklin (ed.), The linguistic situation in the Gulf District and adjacent areas, Papua New Guinea, 149-186. Pacific Linguistics C-26. Canberra: ANU. DOI 10.15144/PL-C26.149 (ANU Open Research hdl 1885/253934, CC BY-SA).
sources.note: Nothing on stress or tone for Pogaia. Four mentions: (i) sec. 4.1, the families of the area share 'the presence of phonemic vowel nasalisation.. a "nasalisation belt". At least the following families are situated in it (from west to east): Awin-Pa, Duna-Pogaia, East Strickland, Bosavi, West and East Kutubu, Teberan, Pawaian..' (a family-level segmental remark, not prosody); (ii) cognate note 'probable cognates in Huli, Duna-Pogaia, and in the East Strickland and Mt. Bosavi families all show a voiced alveodental consonant: wano, pyero, weni, wodo-, walo'; (iii) 'Pogaia: hukan' in a 'skin' cogn…

sources.citation: Shaw, R. Daniel. 1973. A tentative classification of the languages of the Mt Bosavi region (ch. 5, pp. 187-215) and Appendix J.1 Bogaya (p. 589), in Karl J. Franklin (ed.), The linguistic situation in the Gulf District and adjacent areas, Papua New Guinea. Pacific Linguistics C-26.
sources.note: Lexicostatistics only (Duna-Bogaya 20-28%, Huli-Bogaya 5-10%) plus a 100-item Bogaya wordlist in plain orthography with no stress or tone marks. No statement on stress.
